addresses.name: StringHashFind
addresses.comment:
Looks a name up in the engine's own string hash table and answers the stored pointer, or null. **206 direct call sites.**

The table is `{int count; unsigned bucketCount; void** buckets;}` at +0/+4/+8 and a node is `{void* value; Node* next;}`. The hash is the engine's string hash, `h = (h + c) * 61` over the length of the key (`imul eax,eax,0x3D`, the same three bytes inlined at 23 places in the image), reduced by `div [table+4]`. Each node in the bucket is compared by taking `value + 8` as an `Hoi3CString` and running the 4-bytes-at-a-time compare at 0x15F70 over `min(keylen, storedlen)` characters, with the lengths broken as the tie - so **the key is a member of the stored object, at +8**, and nothing is copied into the table.

That +8 is what fixes this instantiation of what is otherwise a template body: the insert half at 0x5C87C0 is the same table and the same hash with the key at value+4. The table itself is a member of whatever owns it (`esi+0x10` of a global at 0x4CDCE7, `vf[0x44]() + 0x6BCF0` at 0x406B5A), and the value is used as a polymorphic object straight afterwards (`mov edx,[eax]; mov ecx,eax; call [edx+0x48]`), so this is the by-name index the loaders go through when a script names a thing.

No class on the name deliberately: the body is shared by several owners, it is in no virtual table, and which class the values belong to is not settled here.

addresses.name: CTrigger::GetBlockText
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __thiscall CTrigger::GetBlockText(CTrigger* this, Hoi3CString* out, CEventScope* scope, bool redWhen, int depth)
addresses.comment:
**Slot 9, and the whole of how a requirement tooltip is drawn.** One line per child:

    indent(depth) + icon + the child's content

where the icon is `(§R*§W)` or `(§G*§W)` by comparing the child's `Evaluate` against **`redWhen`** - the result that counts as unmet, 0 normally and 1 inside a `not`. The parent indents the line, icon and all.

This base walks the children and calls each child's **GetText** (slot 8) for its one line; a child that is itself a block answers empty there, and the walk falls back to the child's own slot 9. A trigger with no children answers the empty string, which is what makes that fallback work.

**Three BiceLib patches land in its `and` and `or` overrides** - see Hooks/EffectText/TriggerIndentText.hpp.

addresses.name: BaseBlockChildBranch
addresses.comment:
`je` past the leaf line to the block path, inside `CTrigger::GetBlockText`. The block path draws **neither indent nor icon** - it goes straight to the child's own slot 9 - which is why a nested `and` or `or` inside a scope used to come out with no asterisk at all.

**BiceLib retargets this branch** (the condition is kept, only the destination changes) to a stub that draws the indent and the asterisk for a block child and then rejoins at `0x5D05DA`.

addresses.name: CAndTrigger::GetBlockText
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __thiscall CAndTrigger::GetBlockText(CAndTrigger* this, Hoi3CString* out, CEventScope* scope, bool redWhen, int depth)
addresses.comment:
Slot 9 of the trigger vftable. One line per child - `indent(depth) + icon + the child's content` - where the icon is a red or green asterisk by whether the child evaluates to `redWhen`. **The parent indents the line, icon and all**, which is why a child that indents itself again comes out adrift.

**The root of a technology's requirements**: an `allow` block is an implicit `and`, so this is the call that has the whole finished tree in hand. Four BiceLib patches land in it - its header indent, its per-child indent, the depth it gives a block child, and its exit.

addresses.name: AndBlockNoHeaderAtTop
addresses.comment: **An `and` at depth 0 draws no header.** `jne` past this and it renders `AND_TRIGGER_STARTS` and its children; fall through and it hands the whole call to `CTrigger::GetBlockText` instead. That is why a technology's `allow`, which is an implicit `and` at the top, lists its conditions without an `All of the below:` above them.

addresses.name: AndHeaderIndentLoop
addresses.comment: The `jle` past an `and` header's own indent loop. **A BiceLib patch site**: one byte to `jmp`, because the parent has already indented this line and the header indenting itself again is what pushed the text right of its icon.

addresses.name: AndBlockChildDepth
addresses.comment: What an `and` passes as the depth when a child is itself a block. The game sends a constant, so a block inside a block restarted at the same level; BiceLib sends the `and`'s own depth plus one.

addresses.name: AndPerChildIndent
addresses.comment: Where an `and` reads its depth as the number of indents to put before each child's line. **A BiceLib patch site**: it wants `depth + 1`, since the children sit *inside* the block, and using the block's own depth left every condition level with its header.

addresses.name: AndTriggerExit
addresses.comment:
`mov ecx, [esp + 0xE4]`, the last instruction of `CAndTrigger::GetBlockText` before its epilogue, and the point every path through the function converges on - two branches inside it land exactly here.

**BiceLib stands here to scroll a requirement tooltip too tall for the screen**: the finished text is in `esi` and the frame is still up, so lines can be taken off the front before the tooltip sees it. One instruction before the epilogue rather than over it, because the epilogue writes `fs:[0]` and reproducing that from inline assembly is a warning and a SAFESEH question nobody needs.

addresses.name: COrTrigger::GetBlockText
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __thiscall COrTrigger::GetBlockText(COrTrigger* this, Hoi3CString* out, CEventScope* scope, bool redWhen, int depth)
addresses.comment:
Slot 9 of the trigger vftable. One line per child - `indent(depth) + icon + the child's content` - where the icon is a red or green asterisk by whether the child evaluates to `redWhen`. **The parent indents the line, icon and all**, which is why a child that indents itself again comes out adrift.

Unlike the `and`, an `or` draws an icon for its own header when nothing above it has - which is why its header indent is skipped with a jump rather than by zeroing the depth the test reads.

addresses.name: OrHeaderIndentLoop
addresses.comment: The same for `or`. **A BiceLib patch site**, one byte to `jmp`.

addresses.name: OrBlockOwnIconAtTop
addresses.comment: **An `or` draws an icon for its own header only at depth 0**, where nothing above it has drawn one; `jne` skips it at any other depth. The test reads the same register the header's indent loop counts down, which is why BiceLib's indent patch has to disable that loop rather than zero the register - zeroing it made every nested `or` draw a second asterisk.

addresses.name: OrBlockChildDepth
addresses.comment: The same for an `or`, which sends its own constant - 1 rather than the `and`'s 0, which is why the two containers drifted differently.

addresses.name: OrPerChildIndent
addresses.comment: The same for `or`. **A BiceLib patch site.**

addresses.name: CNotTrigger::GetBlockText
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __thiscall CNotTrigger::GetBlockText(CNotTrigger* this, Hoi3CString* out, CEventScope* scope, bool redWhen, int depth)
addresses.comment: **`not` renders by flipping the polarity and standing aside**: `cmp byte [ebp+0x10], 0 / sete dl` turns `redWhen` into its opposite and hands the same call to `CTrigger::GetBlockText`. So everything under a `not` is drawn green when it is false. That is what proves the third argument is the polarity and not, say, a count.

addresses.name: NotTriggerEpilogue
addresses.comment:
The epilogue of `CNotTrigger::GetBlockText`, which BiceLib replaces whole.

A `not` flips `redWhen` and forwards to the base **with the depth unchanged**, so the base indents the condition inside it a second time - into the middle of a line the parent has already placed. No depth fixes that: the base draws the icon when the depth is 0 or arrived negative and the indent whenever it is above 0, so "neither" is not a value it can be given. The stub takes the leading indent off the finished text instead.

addresses.name: CContextTrigger::GetBlockText
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __thiscall CContextTrigger::GetBlockText(CContextTrigger* this, Hoi3CString* out, CEventScope* scope, bool redWhen, int depth)
addresses.comment:
The renderer behind **a plain country tag, `controller = { ... }` and `owner = { ... }`** - a scope that hands its conditions a real country to be evaluated against.

That is what makes it the exception among the scopes: BiceLib negates the depth it passes down (`0x5D20A1`), which is the engine's own way of saying "indent this, and still colour the conditions". The iterating scopes cannot have that - their conditions are about a province while the scope passes the country, so an asterisk there would always be red.

addresses.name: ContextTriggerHeaderIndent
addresses.comment: Its own indent loop, at the top of the renderer and before a word of its own text - so it indents a line its parent has already placed, and the text ends up adrift of its own asterisk. **BiceLib turns the `jle` that guards it into an unconditional `jmp`**, which skips the loop and leaves the depth register for the icon test that reads it next.

addresses.name: ContextTriggerChildDepth
addresses.comment: Where `CContextTrigger` hands its conditions their depth: `inc ecx`, so `depth + 1`. **BiceLib makes it `not ecx`**, which is `-(depth + 1)` exactly - the same number, carrying the engine's own flag for "and these conditions can be coloured". The sign is read at the top of `CTrigger::GetBlockText`, which negates it back and remembers that it did.

addresses.name: CAndTrigger::GetText
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __thiscall GetText(CTrigger* this, Hoi3CString* out, CEventScope* scope, int unknown1, int unknown2)
addresses.comment:
**Slot 8 for every container and every scope**: `CAndTrigger` declares it and `COrTrigger`, `CNotTrigger` and all six scope triggers inherit it, because they all derive from `CAndTrigger`. It answers the empty string.

That empty answer is the whole mechanism behind how a tree is walked: a parent asks each child for its one line here, and a child with no line of its own says nothing, which is what sends the parent to the child's block renderer at slot 9 instead.

`CTrigger`'s own slot 8 is `_purecall` (`0x7961D5`), so GetText is pure virtual on the base and this is the first real implementation.

addresses.name: CPureRevoltRiskTrigger::Evaluate
addresses.comment: Slot 6 of vftable 0x15F8814. The same as CRevoltRiskTrigger::Evaluate but **without the MINIMUM_REVOLT_RISK floor**: GetProvinceEffectiveRevoltRisk compared straight against value (+0x40) times 1000. addresses.name: CRevoltRiskTrigger::Evaluate

So the script's revolt_risk = N reads the figure the player sees. Signature corrected 2026-10-02 by the signature audit (reversing/findings/FINDINGS-sigaudit.md).

addresses.name: CCombatModifierTrigger::Evaluate
addresses.comment: **The only reader of CCombatant's per-id modifier flag array (+0x08 + id), and it is a script trigger.** CCombatModifierTrigger slot 6; CTrigger's slot 6 is the pure-virtual stub 0x7961D5, so slot 6 is Evaluate. The class derives from CStringTrigger, which supplies the key as a std::string at +0x40. The body loops id = 0 .. 0x1D (`cmp eax, 0x1e` at 0x607F2C), calls CombatModifierKey (0x164060) into a temporary at [ebp-0x2c], compares it against this->+0x40 through 0x15F70, and on a match reads `scope->+0x40` (the CCombatant) and returns `[combatant + id + 8]` at 0x607F53. No match returns false at 0x607F37. Because the index is computed, no scan for a literal displacement can see this read - which is why every one of the 30 flag bytes looked write-only.

addresses.name: CombatModifierTrigger_ReadFlagArray
addresses.comment: `mov al, byte ptr [edx + eax + 8]` - the single read of CCombatant::modifier_used anywhere in the image. edx is `scope->+0x40`, the CCombatant; eax is the modifier id the trigger's key matched. A whole-image scan for byte accesses of the shape [base + index*1 + 8] finds **twelve** instructions, and this is the only one on a combatant.

addresses.name: CCombatIsConvoyTrigger::Evaluate
addresses.comment: CCombatIsConvoyTrigger slot 6, `ret 4`. Reads `scope->+0x40` (the CCombatant), then `combatant->combat (+0x3C)->+0x2B` and compares that byte against the trigger's own +0x40 byte. Second independent witness that a combat trigger's scope holds the CCombatant at +0x40, and that CCombat +0x2B is the convoy flag - the same byte CNavalCombatant::Attack tests to switch a ship's sea_attack for its convoy_attack.

addresses.name: CCombatIsWinnerTrigger::Evaluate
addresses.comment: CCombatIsWinnerTrigger slot 6, `ret 4`. `combatant = scope->+0x40`; returns false unless `combatant->combat (+0x3C)->+0x2A` is set, then calls **CCombatant slot 16** (0x1656F0 on the base, ReturnFalse on the three target combatants) and compares the answer against the trigger's own +0x40 byte. Third witness for scope +0x40, and it is what identifies CCombatant slot 16 as the is-winner predicate and CCombat +0x2A as the byte that says the result is decided.

addresses.name: GetDiploScoreFromLua
addresses.signature: int __cdecl GetDiploScoreFromLua(const char* lua_function, CCountryTag* actor, CCountryTag* recipient, CCountryTag* recipient_again, CCountryTag recipient_value, int extra)
addresses.comment:
**The engine asking the mod's Lua what the AI thinks of a diplomatic offer.** Six arguments, cdecl - every caller does `add esp, 0x18` - the first being the name of a Lua function, and the score comes back in eax. There are exactly 14 `DiploScore_*` literals in the image and every one is passed to this function; all 14 are defined in the mod, twelve in script/ai_diplomacy.lua plus DiploScore_OfferTrade in ai_trade.lua and DiploScore_LicenceTechnology in ai_license.lua.

Three things happen here. **It returns 100 without calling Lua** when the acting country's id equals g_CCurrentGameState +0xC34 (player) and the byte at 0x1A8562F is set, so a script's opinion of what the human offers is never consulted down this path. **It resolves an AI object as CCountry +0x1D8**, trying three tags and taking the first non-null - the recipient, then the actor, then the recipient's other pointer - each through CCountryTag::GetCountry (0x402610). **Then it calls Lua**, 0xA445B0 with the AI pointer, the tags and the name, and 0xA44080 to convert the result to an int.

Named for what it does; no class. See reversing/FINDINGS-diplomacy.md.

**Signature note, 2026-10-01: there is no sixth `int extra` argument.** Arguments five and six are the two dwords of one `CCountryTag` passed by value - the bridge does `lea ecx, [ebp+0x18]; call CCountryTag::GetCountry` at 0xA0DD39, which needs all eight bytes. `recipient_value` is the right name for it. Left in the signature rather than changed, because the argument list's stack layout is what callers are matched against.

addresses.name: GetOfferTradeScoreFromLua
addresses.comment: The widest clone of GetDiploScoreFromLua, sitting immediately after it (the bridge's last `ret` is at 0xA0DDE1) with `DiploScore_OfferTrade` reached through the proxy at 0xA44610. Eight stack dwords, `add esp, 0x20` at its one caller, CTradeAction::GetAIAcceptance. Seven values go to Lua: the CEU3AI, three tags, the CTradeAction and the two seven-float goods blocks. Same player/0x1A8562F short-circuit as the bridge. See reversing/FINDINGS-survivors.md.

addresses.name: CTradeAction::IsValid
addresses.comment: **CTradeAction slot 13**, one holder only (vftable 0x15FB8D4), and slot 13 is `IsValid` across the whole CDiplomaticAction family - see VirtualThunkSlot13. 0xA38770 to the three `ret`s at 0xA388EB/0xA38916/0xA3891E, no stack arguments, `this` in ecx. With actor = countries[this->+0xC] and recipient = countries[this->+0x14] it answers false unless: both have NumberOfOwnedProvinces (+0xCF8) > 0; the pair's CDiplomacyStatus (actor->+0xE28[recipient id]) has no `war` (+0x20); and **neither side has an overlord other than the other party** (+0xF34 set implies +0xF3C must equal the other id). On top of that, a `government_in_exile` (+0x95) side must still hold its acting capital's province (0x42F100 then +0x330 == its own id). All of that only when the action's `value` byte (+0x24) is set; when it is clear the answer is instead FindMatchingTradeRoute(status, &this->route) - i.e. a cancellation is valid only if the identical route already exists. This is the gate FINDINGS-survivors.md saw called at 0xA38B20 from slot 17.

addresses.name: CTradeAction::GetAIAcceptance
addresses.comment: Slot 17 of CTradeAction (vftable 0x15FB8D4); slot 19 begins at 0xA38D20, so the body is 0xA38B00..0xA38D1F and the two `ret`s inside it are early exits, not a boundary (trap 3). Four gates before Lua is asked: `if (this->+0xC == this->+0x14) return 100` (both sides the same country); `if (!slot13()) return 0`, which is the can-offer gate called **from inside** slot 17; `if (!0xA390D0(this)) return 0`; and `if (recipient's CEU3AI::AlreadyTradingDisabledResource(this->+0x28)) return 0`. Then it copies the embedded route's two seven-goods blocks to floats, dividing each by the 1000.0 at 0x160A300, and calls GetOfferTradeScoreFromLua (0xA0DDF0) with eight dwords. Seven values reach Lua, matching ai_trade.lua's DiploScore_OfferTrade(voAI, voFromTag, voToTag, voObserverTag, voTradeAction, voTradedFrom, voTradedTo) parameter for parameter. See reversing/FINDINGS-survivors.md.

It first computes `chargeMoney = !(countries[actor]->+0xDEC && countries[recipient]->+0xDEC)` - the same test as CEU3AI::CanTradeFreeResources - then normalises a negative value to `(v / -1000) * 1000` through the 64-bit helpers, and calls TradeRouteSetTradedOf(&this->route, category, v, side, chargeMoney): once with the **recipient's** tag always, and additionally with the actor's tag first when the value is exactly zero, so setting zero clears both directions.

addresses.name: TradeRouteSetOneGood
addresses.comment: 0xA4C880, two callers, both inside TradeRouteSetTradedOf (0xA4CAC8 and 0xA4CAEB). It writes `(*destBlock)[category] = value`, keeps the delta, and **when the value is positive zeroes the same category in the other direction's block** (`mov [eax + esi*4], 0` at 0xA4C8AB) - so a route cannot move one good both ways. It then reads the pair of globals [0x1710CD0] (+200000) and [0x1710CD4] (-200000) the same way 0xA4C9A0 does. Bare `ret` with the caller doing `add esp, 0x18`, so six stack dwords plus the destination block in EAX; the argument order is read off the two call sites, not off a signature, hence `likely` and no signature recorded.

addresses.name: TradeRouteValueOneGood
addresses.comment: 0xA4C9A0, called twice per goods category from TradeRouteSetTradedOf's money loop (0xA4CB3F and 0xA4CB76), and its result is added into the money entry (index 2) of one of the two blocks. It begins by taking the absolute values of the pair of globals [0x1710CD0] (+200000) and [0x1710CD4] (-200000) and summing them to 400000, then indexes the country database and the pair's CDiplomacyStatus (+0xE28, +0x60). **So this is the price the engine puts on one good in one direction**, and the two globals are its scale. Bare `ret` with the callers doing `add esp, 0x1c`, so seven stack dwords plus register arguments; only the first fifteen instructions were read, hence `inferred` and no signature recorded.

addresses.name: TradeRouteSetTradedOf
addresses.comment: 0xA4CA90 to the `ret 0xC` at 0xA4CB94. Route in EAX and category in EDX, so class-free per trap 11. **It is the function that settles CTradeRoute's two goods blocks**: when `side->id == route->to_id (+0x30)` the value goes into the block at **+0x34** and the other block is +0x44; otherwise - the `from` side - it goes into **+0x44**. So +0x34 belongs to `to` and +0x44 to `from`, the opposite of what project.json records. When `chargeMoney` is set it then zeroes **index 2 of both blocks** (`mov [eax+8], 0`) and recomputes it as a sum over all seven categories through 0xA4C9A0 - so **goods index 2 is money and the engine treats it as the price of the other six, not as a tradeable resource.** That is why CEU3AI::AlreadyTradingResourceOtherWay skips index 2.

addresses.name: std::string::fromCString
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __cdecl std::string::fromCString(Hoi3CString* this@ESI, const char* text@EDX)
addresses.comment: MSVC's `std::basic_string<char>::basic_string(const char*)`, statically linked and given a register calling convention by LTCG: the string is in ESI and the C string in EDX, nothing is on the stack, and `this` comes back in EAX. The body is the textbook two steps. First `_Tidy()` on an *uninitialised* object - `[esi+0x14] = 0xF` (_Myres), `[esi+0x10] = 0` (_Mysize), `[esi] = 0` (_Buf[0]), the same 0x18-byte layout `std::string::assign` at 0xA160 already reads. Then `assign(_Ptr, _Traits::length(_Ptr))`: a four-instruction inline strlen (`lea edi,[eax+1]` / `mov cl,[eax]; inc eax; test cl,cl; jne` / `sub eax,edi`) whose result is pushed with the pointer before `mov ecx,esi; call 0xA160`. **6732 direct call sites**, far more than any other unnamed function left, and it is how every loader, log line and error message turns a literal into a string - the caller is invariably `mov edx,<literal>; lea esi,<fresh local>; call`, followed by the EH state byte being stepped for the new object. There is no null check on EDX, which is what separates the constructor from an assignment.

addresses.name: std::string::operatorPlus
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __thiscall std::string::operatorPlus(Hoi3CString* this, Hoi3CString* out@ESI, Hoi3CString* right@stack:4) @EAX
addresses.comment:
**`std::operator+(const std::string&, const std::string&)`, in its named-return-value form** - previously recorded as `TextBuilder::Append`. There is no TextBuilder: `ecx` is the left-hand string, not a builder object. It calls `std::string::concat` (`0x65CC70`) into a local temporary, tidies `out` (the NRV slot, in esi) to empty and `assignString`s the temporary into it, frees the temporary's heap buffer when its capacity reached 0x10, and answers `out` in eax. `ret 4`.

Call sites chain it exactly the way `a + b + c` compiles: `std::string::operatorPlusChars` produces the first temporary in eax, that becomes this function's `ecx`, and a fresh stack slot is handed in esi for the result (0x40D70E-0x40D726). The `\xa7Y...\xa7W` colour runs the old name described are just one of the things callers happen to concatenate.

addresses.name: std::string::operatorPlusChars
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __cdecl std::string::operatorPlusChars(Hoi3CString* out@ECX, const char* left@EDX, Hoi3CString* right@stack:4) @EAX
addresses.comment:
**`std::operator+(const char*, const std::string&)`** - previously recorded as `TextBuilder::Begin`. There is no TextBuilder: `ecx` is the string the result is built into (the named-return-value slot), `edx` is the literal on the left, and the string on the right is pushed. It inlines `strlen` on `edx`, builds a local Hoi3CString from it with `std::string::assign` (`0xA160`), calls `std::string::operatorPlus` (`0x65B0D0`) with that temporary as the left operand and `out` still in esi, frees the temporary and answers `out` in eax. **The caller cleans the stack** (bare `ret`, `add esp, 4` at the call site), which is why this is written as cdecl with the registers spelled out rather than as fastcall.

This is the head of every `"literal" + str + ...` chain in the game, including the `"\xa7Y" + name + "\xa7W"` colour runs the old name was taken from and the `"File exception: " + what()` at 0x404723.

addresses.name: std::ostream::flush
addresses.comment:
**`std::basic_ostream<char>::flush()`**: `if (!(rdstate() & (failbit|badbit)) && rdbuf()->pubsync() == -1) setstate(badbit); return *this;`. `pubsync` is the streambuf's virtual at `+0x34`; the `-1` answer is the only failure it recognises.

**`this` arrives in ESI, not ECX** - the compiler gave this one a convention of its own, as it did `std::string::operator=` (eax) and `LogRecord::Flush` (eax). Every caller sets esi and nothing else: 0x40A296 (`_Osfx`), 0x409BA8 and 0x421DD8 (the two sentry constructors, flushing `_Tiestr`). Bare `ret`, the stream comes back in eax.

Its body is what `std::endl` at 0x2240 has inlined; the two are the same 25 instructions.

addresses.name: std::ostringstream::ostringstream
addresses.signature: std::ostringstream* __stdcall std::ostringstream::ostringstream(std::ostringstream* stream, int mode, int isMostDerived)
addresses.comment:
`std::basic_ostringstream<char>`'s constructor, shared by the plain stream and by `LogRecord`, which is why it looks the virtual base offset up instead of using a constant: `esi = stream + *(int*)(*stream + 4)` is the `basic_ios`, so the same body works whether that lives at `+0x50` (a plain ostringstream) or at `+0x78` (a LogRecord). When `isMostDerived` is non-zero it also writes its own vbtable `0x160285C` at `+0` and the `ios_base` vftable `0x15A7B9C` at `+0x50`; `LogRecord::LogRecord` passes 0 because it has already written its own. Then `ios_base::_Init` (`0xC7FA0`), `basic_ios._Mystrbuf = stream+4`, `_Tiestr = 0`, `_Fillch = widen(' ')`, the `basic_ios` vftable `0x15FC550`, the stringbuf constructor at `0x10F0E0` with vftable `0x15F2B34`, and finally the stringbuf's `_Seekhigh = 0` and `_Mystate = mode|ios::out` at `stream+0x40`/`stream+0x44`. `ret 0xC`.

**This is what fixes the class's field boundaries:** for a plain ostringstream the virtual base sits at `+0x50`, so the vbptr plus the `basic_stringbuf` occupy exactly `0..0x4F`, and `LogRecord`'s own four fields are what push its `basic_ios` out to `+0x78`.

addresses.name: std::ostringstream::str
addresses.comment: `ostringstream::str()`, register convention: the stream in ecx, the string to fill in eax. All it does is `add ecx,4` to reach the `basic_stringbuf` and call `0x520940`, then answer the out string. Bare `ret`, nothing on the stack. `LogRecord::FlushAndDestruct` calls this to get the accumulated message before handing it to the sink.

addresses.name: std::string::concat
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __cdecl std::string::concat(Hoi3CString* out, Hoi3CString* left, Hoi3CString* right) @EAX

It tidies `out` to the empty state (`_Myres = 0xF`, `_Mysize = 0`, `out[0] = 0`), reserves `left.length + right.length` through `0x1D50`, then `appendString(out, left, 0, -1)` and `appendString(out, right, 0, -1)`. addresses.name: LogRecord::LogRecord

addresses.comment: Builds the object one log line is assembled in. In order: the vbtable pointer `0x15FCE98` at `+0`, the `ios_base` vftable `0x15A7B9C` at `+0x78`, `std::ostringstream::ostringstream(record, 2 /*ios::out*/, 0)` at `0x65BBA0` for the stream half, the `basic_ios` vftable `0x15FCE94` written through the vbtable, then **the sink at `+0x50`**, **the source file at `+0x54`** (an `Hoi3CString`, filled by `std::string::assignString(record+0x54, file, 0, -1)`), **the line at `+0x70`** and **the channel at `+0x74`**. The message is accumulated into the stream part afterwards by `operator<<`. `ret 0x14`; the record comes back in eax. Reached from `LogRecord::Make` through `LogRecord::Construct` (`0x6649D0`), which is what supplies the five stack arguments.

addresses.name: LogRecord::ScalarDeletingDestructor
addresses.comment: MSVC's `??_G` for the record: `this` arrives as `record+0x78` (the `basic_ios` virtual base, the same thing `FlushAndDestruct` takes), it recovers the record with `lea edi,[ecx-0x78]`, runs `LogRecord::FlushAndDestruct` and then `~ios_base` (`0x794BAE`), and frees the record only when bit 0 of `flags` is set. `ret 4`, record back in eax. Sits in no virtual table - `vtable.py --holding 0xA64790` finds none - so nothing dispatches to it; it is the out-of-line copy the compiler emitted anyway.

addresses.name: LogRecord::FlushAndDestruct
addresses.comment:
The body of `~LogRecord` - the destructor of the ostringstream-derived temporary every log line in the game is built into, inlined at 679 call sites. **Its argument is not the record: it is `record + 0x78`**, the `std::basic_ios` virtual base, and every field is reached at a negative displacement from it, so a reader has to subtract 0x78 to get back to the object. `LogRecordIosBase` is a deliberately separate type for that sub-object rather than `LogRecord*`, because a `LogRecord*` here would render `record+0x50` as `-0x28` into the wrong struct.

It (1) writes the basic_ios vftable 0x15FCE94 through the vbtable at `record+0`, (2) calls `std::ostringstream::str` (`0x65BD10`) to pull the message out of the stringbuf at `record+4`, (3) copies that into a second local string with `std::string::assign`, (4) makes the sink call `(*(*[record+0x50]))[1](channel=[record+0x74], file=record+0x54, line=[record+0x70], message=&text)` - slot 1 of the sink at `record+0x50`, which FINDINGS-script.md already records as `LogSink::Write(channel, file, line, message)` with exactly that field layout, (5) frees both temporaries and the file string at `record+0x54`, and (6) tears the stream back down, vftable 0x15FC550 for the ios base, 0x15F2B34 on the stringbuf at `record+4` before 0x6D1360 and 0x10CD90 destroy it, and 0x15A7B94 last. It does **not** run the final `ios_base` destructor; the caller does, which is why `LogRecord::Flush` at 0x24B0 is only `lea esi,[eax+0x78]; push esi; call this; mov [esi],0x15A7B8C; call 0x794BAE` and why all 679 inline sites repeat that same two-step tail. This is the reason the two targets share so many *::LoadKey callers without sharing all of them: 0x65A7A0 builds the message, this one emits it.

addresses.name: LogRecord::Construct
addresses.signature: LogRecord* __stdcall LogRecord::Construct(LogRecord* record@ESI, int line@ECX, int channel@EAX, LogSink* sink, Hoi3CString* file) @EAX
addresses.comment: The register-convention forwarder LTCG left between `LogRecord::Make` and the constructor at `0x6646E0`: it takes the record in esi, the line in ecx and the channel in eax, the sink and the file on the stack, and pushes all five in the order the `__stdcall` constructor wants (`record, sink, file, line, channel`). Returns the record in eax. `ret 8` - it cleans only the two it was given on the stack.

addresses.name: std::ostream::writeCString
addresses.signature: std::ostream* __cdecl std::ostream::writeCString(std::ostream* os@ESI, const char* text@EDX) @EAX
addresses.comment:
**`os.write(text, strlen(text))` for a NUL-terminated string**, and the `<<` that 427 call sites use to put a C string into the game's log. `strlen` is open-coded as the four-instruction byte scan at `0xA64A10`; the length and a zero high dword are then pushed with the pointer and the stream and `std::ostream::write` (`0x664A30`) is called. It answers the stream in `eax` so the idiom chains: `LogRecord::Make(file, line, channel) << "text" << ... << endl`.

**The convention is one the optimiser invented, not `__cdecl` as written on a page.** Both arguments arrive in registers - the stream in `esi` (never saved, never reloaded: the epilogue is `mov eax, esi`) and the string in `edx` (`mov eax, edx` is the first thing the body does) - and the function ends in a bare `ret` having consumed nothing from the stack. `0x434389` is a plain example: `mov edx, 0x15B65D0 ('Bad messagetype'); mov esi, eax; call 0xA64A00; push eax; call std::endl`. This is the same re-signing that gave `std::string::fromCString` (`0x65A7A0`) its `this@ESI, text@EDX` and `std::ostream::flush` (`0x65BB20`) its `this@ESI`.

**It is not `std::operator<<Chars` (`0x21D30`), and the difference is real.** `0x21D30` is MSVC's `_Insert_string`: it reads `ios_base::_Wide` at `+0x20/+0x24`, computes the padding, emits `_Fillch` from `+0x40` and finishes with `width(0)`. This one does none of that - it goes straight to `write`, so a stream with a non-zero `width()` formats differently through the two. **What I could not settle** is whether that makes it a second `operator<<(ostream&, const char*)` from a translation unit built against a different `<ostream>`, or an engine-local unpadded fast inserter; the name records what it does rather than deciding that.

The four call sites that do not load `edx` from a string literal are the reason this wrapper exists at all: where the length is not a compile-time constant the compiler cannot fold it, so it calls the scanner instead of `write` directly.

addresses.name: MakeFixedToken
addresses.comment: Builds a tok_fixed (0xD) CToken in the caller's buffer from a thousandths integer: divides by 1000, formats `%d.%03d`, and handles a value between -999 and 0 by writing the sign separately (`-%d.%03d` at VA 0x15FD138) so that -1 comes out `-0.001` rather than `0.-001`. This is the one place the game's thousandths convention becomes text. Returns the buffer in EAX.

addresses.name: TokenToFixedPoint
addresses.comment:
Turns a `CToken`'s text into the engine's thousandths fixed point: `*out = atoi(text) * 1000 + fraction`, where `fraction` is the digits after the first `.` read as a number and then padded with zeros to exactly three places - `1.5` gives 1500, `1.25` gives 1250, `2` gives 2000, and a token with no `.` at all gives a fraction of 0. The sign comes from `text[0]`: when it is `-` and `atoi` returned 0 the fraction is negated anyway, so `-0.5` comes out -500.

The `imul 1000` / `__allmul(x,1000)` / `__alldiv(x,1000000)` round trip in the middle is a 64 bit overflow guard on a fraction with more than three digits, not a second scaling - `lea edx,[eax+0x189373]; cmp edx,0x39580D` picks the 32 bit path only when `eax*1000` cannot overflow, and both paths hand the same fraction back. The fast path's `0x431BDE83` with `sar edx,0x12` is the standard divide-by-1000000 magic (2^50/10^6 = 1125899906.8).

**188 direct call sites, all loaders**, and the argument is `parse + 0x228` (`CParseContext::value`, the CToken) at every one looked at. It takes the token, not the context, so it reports nothing: a token that is not a number simply gives 0. It answers `out` in eax so the caller can read the value straight back - `call; mov eax,[eax]; mov [ebx+0xC4],eax` at 0x4CDE8B, and `call; movd xmm0,[eax]; cvtdq2ps; divsd [0x160A300]` (1000.0) at 0x4B1F93, which is the float the loader actually wanted.

addresses.name: Tokenizer::Tokenizer
addresses.comment: Builds the tokenizer a file is read through: 0x114 bytes, vftable 0x11FD1FC, taking the path. Slot 1 is what the parse loops call for the next token. No RTTI, so the class name is BiceLib's.

addresses.name: RegisterDynamicToken
addresses.comment: **Turns a key loaded from a file into a SaveToken**, so the save code can write it as a number like any compiled-in key. Looks the text up in the map at `g_dynamic_tokens` and adds it if it is new; its failure message is `"Error on dynamic token: "`. These ids are **not** in `ghidra/saveTokens.json`, which holds only the compiled ones - reversing/saveTokens.py reads the live table that has both. The name is BiceLib's.

addresses.name: BuildTokenTable
addresses.comment: Fills the id to key table once, out of the CToken array at g_save_tokens - 2138 of them, each carrying its own id - and a list of ones registered later, which is everything the loaded mod defines. The table only exists in a running game, which is why reversing/saveTokens.py reads it out of the process.

addresses.name: TokenText
addresses.comment: The key a token id stands for, as a std::string built into the caller's buffer: the id indexes the table at g_save_tokens_first. Builds that table on first use. This is the lookup that turns `mov ecx, 0x522` into carrier_size.

addresses.name: FileExists
addresses.comment: Answers whether a path is there; the `common/` loader calls it once per file to choose between the mod's copy and vanilla's, and CCountry::LoadOobFile for the same reason. The path arrives in **eax** - the compiler kept the function to itself - and it reads the string's capacity at `+0x14` to find the characters. The name is BiceLib's, from that use.

addresses.name: ListFilesWithExtension
addresses.comment: The directory enumerator the engine uses whenever a stage reads a whole folder rather than a named file: called twice with '.gfx' (0x631321, 0x631370), twice with '.gui' (0x631CFC, 0x631D45), twice with '.txt' by technology phase 2 (0x540FD8, 0x541027), and once each for music/ (0x638B7F) and scenarios/ (0x63941D). Twice each time because there are two search directories, the mod's and vanilla's; 0x794A40 merges the two lists. Argument order is **inferred** from the call sites, not from the body.

addresses.name: CBinaryStream::Checksum
addresses.comment: length -1 means the whole stream (size through vftable slot 14, [vf+0x38]). Reads in 0x40000-byte chunks and runs a Fletcher-32 with modulus 0xFFFF and a subtract-once reduction: a += byte; if (a > 0xFFFF) a -= 0xFFFF; b += a; if (b > 0xFFFF) b -= 0xFFFF; returning (a << 16) | b with both accumulators starting at 0. Reimplemented in Python it reproduces the mod's map/cache/time exactly for seven files, and the base game's for a different seven.

addresses.name: SaveWriteFixed
addresses.signature: void __stdcall SaveWriteFixed(SaveToken key@ECX, CSaveWriter* writer@EDI, int thousandths@stack:4)
addresses.comment: **Not SaveWriteInt.** Writes `<key>=<n>.<nnn>` and a newline for a value the game holds in thousandths: SaveWriteKey, then a CToken, then SaveWriteToken(tok_newline). In a text save it hands the int to MakeFixedToken, which formats it `%d.%03d` as tok_fixed (0xD); in a binary save (writer->binary set) it formats the raw int `%d` as tok_int (0xC) instead, so no precision is lost either way. The writer arrives in EDI, not ESI as in the plain-int sibling at 0x678CA0 - the compiler picked a register per function, so the call sites decide.

addresses.signature: void __stdcall SaveWriteNamedFixed(Hoi3CString* key@EAX, CSaveWriter* writer@EDI, int thousandths@stack:4)
addresses.comment: SaveWriteFixed for a key that is not a token: the key is a runtime string, so it open-codes what SaveWriteKey does - indent by depth-1, write the name as a tok_word, write tok_equals - and then writes the value exactly as SaveWriteFixed does, `%d.%03d` as tok_fixed in a text save and `%d` as tok_int in a binary one, followed by a newline. This is how a save writes rows keyed by a moddable name rather than by a built-in token.

No binary branch - an integer is an integer in both formats. Only four call sites, because most integer keys are written by hand as SaveWriteKey + SaveWriteValue inside the SaveContents itself.

addresses.name: ParseFixedPoint
addresses.comment:
The fixed point reader of the `*::LoadKey` family, beside `ParseInt` (0x67B470), `ParseBool` and `ParseString`: `*out` gets the value token as thousandths. Both arguments are in registers, so there is nothing on the stack and the function ends in a bare `ret`.

It takes one of two readings, decided by the tokenizer's virtual slot 2 - `mov ecx,[parse+0x1C]; mov eax,[ecx]; call [eax+8]`, on the field project.json already calls `CParseContext::tokenizer`. That slot is `_purecall` in the tokenizer base (vftable 0x15FD1F0, slots 1 and 2 both 0xB961D5) and a compile time constant in each subclass, so it is a kind flag, not a computation: the tokenizer used everywhere for files (vftable 0x15FD1FC, 78 construction sites) answers **false** through `xor al,al; ret` at 0x192360, and the rarer one (vftable 0x15FD208, 4 sites, all reached from the 0xB3xxxx network module) answers **true** through `mov al,1; ret` at 0x692590.

True takes the text as already scaled - `sscanf(parse->value.text, "%i", out)` straight into `*out`. False sends `&parse->value` to 0x6696A0, which is the checked form of `TokenToFixedPoint`: `sscanf("%i")` for the whole part, `strstr(text, ".")` for a fraction, the first three fraction digits zero-padded, and the whole thing multiplied by 1000 - so the `1.5` a script file writes becomes 1500. Either reading failing ends in `ReportParseError(parse@ESI)`, which esi already holds.

**76 direct call sites**, the switch arm shape being `mov eax,[ebp+8]; lea edi,[<field>]; call` with the caller's `ret 8` right after (0x414FB4, 0x4CD030).

addresses.name: ParsePoint
addresses.comment: Reads an `{ x = .. y = .. }` block. Checks the value is a block (`[parse +0x1C] +0xC == 3`) and reports a parse error if not. CAlignment's only key, `position`, is one of these. The register is **inferred**.

addresses.name: CParseContext::FreeMessages
addresses.comment:
Walks the message list freeing each node and its two strings, then clears first, last and count. The destructor calls it, and **nothing is logged on the way out** - which is why the mod's `common/` files never produce a line however many unknown keys they carry.

**It has no receiver anywhere.** ECX is dead at entry - the first instruction is `mov eax,[ebp+8]` - and dead at the call: CParseContext::~CParseContext (0x67A630) passes `this+4` on the stack having clobbered ECX in a `free` two instructions earlier, and `ret 4` cleans that one argument. So it is a free helper over the list head, not a member with its receiver in a register. The list itself **is** a CParseContext field: the destructor's argument is `this+4` and the site at 0x67C354 passes `[ebp+8]+4` of a CParseContext it is handed, so the head is messages_first/messages_last/messages_count at CParseContext +4/+8/+0xC. A node is two Hoi3CStrings, at +0 and +0x20, with the next pointer at +0x40 - not a LinkedListNode, which is why the parameter is typed for this list rather than as CList*.

addresses.name: CCommand::LoadKey
addresses.signature: void __thiscall CCommand::LoadKey(CCommand* this, CParseContext* parse, SaveToken key)
addresses.comment: **The keys its switch names**, 3 of them, one case each: `identity`, `istargetasynchronous`, `tickstamp`. Inherited by 4 classes in all. Read from the switch by reversing/definitions.py. A loader may resolve further keys as names out of a database - CGovernment and CMinister both do - but anything that is neither is dropped in silence.

addresses.name: CPersistent::Load
addresses.comment:
**Slot 3 of CPersistent, and the load half of the persistence pair.** Renamed: this was recorded as `CParseContext::ReportMessages`, which described only its error tail. It sits in **748 vftable slots, every one of them slot 3, across 747 classes** - the same classes whose slot 1 is CPersistent::Save (rva 0x5BB10, 749 slots, 748 of them at index 1). A function in 748 slots is a shared base-class method, so `this` is the persistent object and the CParseContext is its **argument**, not its `this`.

Extent 0xA7C050..0xA7C39F with **two `ret 4` exits** and int3 padding at 0xA7C3A2. The first `ret` at 0xA7C11A is the success path; the cold path from 0xA7C11D shares the same frame (it uses esi and [esp+0x1B4] against the `sub esp, 0x1A0` at the top) and is not a separate function, though it looks like one. Reading the two as separate bodies is the mistake this entry used to encode.

What it does before any reporting: takes the parse context, reads its `+0x1C` file object, and if that object's `+0x110` is clear calls its slot 1, storing the result at `+8` and writing 0x13 to `+0xC` when it comes back null, then marks `+0x110`. It then copies 0x104 bytes - a MAX_PATH path - out of `+0xC` onto the stack. Only the cold path joins the messages through CParseContext::MessagesAsText (0x67AB40) and logs them under `persistent.cpp` as `Error: "` ... `" near line: ` ... `" in file: "`.

**Seven direct callers** - CGameState::LoadKey (a savegame), CUnitPlan::LoadKey, CSetPlanObjectivesCommand::LoadKey, the bookmarks loader at 0x1CBB0, and three DLC and competitive-mode paths - but the 748 slots mean it is also reached virtually. The old entry concluded from the seven callers alone that **a bad key in a mod's data file is dropped in total silence**; that conclusion now needs redoing, because a virtual slot 3 is reachable from every persistent class. What has not changed is that an unknown key may simply never produce a parse message in the first place - see FINDINGS-script.md.

addresses.name: LoadKey_ReportUnknown
addresses.signature: void __stdcall LoadKey_ReportUnknown(void* this@ECX, CParseContext* parse, SaveToken key)
addresses.comment: A tail call to ReportUnknownKey and nothing else: the LoadKey a class gets when it has no keys of its own to try. The linker folded it across 75 unrelated classes - CColor among them, which is why it was recorded as CColor::LoadKey - so it belongs to none of them. **It has no keys at all** - the whole body is a tail call to ReportUnknownKey. A colour is three numbers in a row, `color = { 139 90 43 }`, read positionally by the block loader rather than by key. **The body is shared by 75 unrelated classes**, so "no keys" is the answer for all of them and the body is not CColor's property.

addresses.name: CGui::LoadKey
addresses.comment: **The whole grammar of a `.gui` file, and it is one key.** Inherited unchanged by CEU3Gui (slot 4 of its CPersistent vftable 0x15CD7D8). `cmp [ebp+0xC], 0x7B` - token 123, `guitypes` - and **every other token is dropped in silence**. The match calls 0xA7DF60 with the parse context, `CGui+0x34` (the gui-type registry) and `CGui+0xC` (the CFactory base that knows which CGuiType subclass each inner keyword builds); note `ecx` inside this function is the CPersistent subobject at CGui+4, so the `lea ecx,[ecx-4]` / `lea eax,[ecx+8]` / `add ecx,0x30` are CGui+0, +0xC and +0x34. **The oracle agrees exactly**: 52 of the 54 top-level keys in the mod's `interface/*.gui` are `guiTypes`, and the two files that instead open with `windowType` or `instantTextBoxType` at column 0 load nothing at all.
addresses.signature: void __thiscall CGui::LoadKey(CGui* this, CParseContext* parse, SaveToken key)

addresses.name: CEU3Gui::GetGuiType
addresses.comment: **This is how you find a window by name.** TGui slot 18 (`+0x48`), held by CEU3Gui's vftable 0x15CD754 and by CGui's 0x15FDA10. Five instructions: `add ecx,0x34; mov eax,[ecx]; mov eax,[eax+4]; jmp eax` - a tail call through slot 1 of the embedded registry at CGui+0x34, whose vftable is 0x1602108, reaching 0x6ACE70 and then the tree walk at rva 0x67E030. Returns the CGuiType or null. **It is not a StringHashFind table** and the match is case-insensitive. The caller gets the CEU3Gui from CInGameIdler slot 14 (rva 0x24D7E0); CInGameIdler::Enter does exactly this for `unitlist_start` and `unitlist_offset` at 0x65A331 and 0x65A3BC. The types live for the whole process after startup, so the pointer is safe to hold.

addresses.name: GuiTypeTree_Find
addresses.comment: Slot 2 of the gui-type registry's vftable 0x1602108. `cmp [ecx+4],0` - the tree's root is at registry+4, i.e. **CGui +0x38** - and returns null for an empty tree, otherwise tail-jumps to the walk at rva 0x67E030 with the root in eax.
addresses.signature: void* __thiscall GuiTypeTree_Find(void* tree, const char* name@stack:4)

addresses.name: CGui_LoadGuiTypes
addresses.signature: void __stdcall CGui_LoadGuiTypes(CParseContext* parse@stack:4, void* registry@stack:8, void* factory@stack:0xC)
addresses.comment: The body of the `guiTypes` block, and the only caller is CGui::LoadKey (rva 0x67D700). Its three arguments are the parse context, `&CGui+0x34` (the ternary search tree) and `CGui+0xC` (the CFactory base) - which is the whole shape of the mechanism, since the registry is non-empty by the time CEU3Gui::GetGuiType is called. **`inferred`: the body was not read.** What it would settle is whether a duplicate gui-type name replaces the earlier one or is dropped, which is a live modding question. Signature corrected 2026-10-02 by the signature audit (reversing/findings/FINDINGS-sigaudit.md).

addresses.name: TernarySearchTreeFind
addresses.comment: **The GUI registry's lookup, and it is a ternary search tree, not a hash.** Node layout `{void* value; char key; Node* low; Node* high; Node* equal;}` at +0, +4, +8, +0xC, +0x10. Per character it calls tolower (0xB96692) on the query byte and subtracts the node's byte: equal and end-of-string returns `[[esi]]`, equal with more to go descends `+0x10` and advances, greater goes to `+0xC`, less to `+8`, and a null child returns 0. **The comparison is case-insensitive**, so two gui types whose names differ only in case collide, and the loader gives no warning. Nothing about this body is specific to gui types; it is a template body like StringHashFind.
addresses.signature: void* __fastcall TernarySearchTreeFind(void** root@EAX, const char* name@stack:4)

addresses.name: ReturnZero
addresses.comment:
`xor eax, eax; ret` - the shared stub the compiler folds every trivial `return 0` onto. It appears in **189 vftable slots across 81 classes**, so finding it in a slot says only that the class does not implement that method, never what the method is for. Worth knowing where it lands: five diplomatic actions - CGuaranteeAction, CInfluenceNation, CInfluenceAllianceLeader, CShareTechnologyAction and CNullDiplomaticAction - point slot 17, GetAIAcceptance, at it, so **their AI acceptance is a hard zero and no script is asked**. That is why the mod's own DiploScore_Guarantee and DiploScore_InfluenceNation are called from ai_foreign_minister.lua rather than by the engine. See reversing/FINDINGS-diplomacy.md.

**Corrected 2026-10-01: it is six diplomatic actions, not five.** `CDeclareWarAction` points slot 17 here too. Counted straight off the vftables across the whole 24-class family, which also found that family larger than recorded - `CWarGoalBaseAction` has three children nobody had enumerated. See reversing/FINDINGS-survivors.md.

addresses.name: SharedEmptyStub_A806D0
addresses.comment:
A shared do-nothing stub in 336 vftable slots across the image - **not** to be named after any one domain. Recorded here only because it is **CCombatant slot 21**, and all five ApplyCombatModifiers overrides call `this->slot 21(unit, other)` immediately before their night block (land 0x16A9C1, naval 0x166BD6, air 0x16D159, bomber 0x162174, target 0x162E2C). No combatant overrides it, so that call does nothing in this build - it is an extension point nobody implemented, and anyone reading those functions should not go looking for a body.

**The rva was recorded as 0xA806D0, which is this stub's virtual address.** Corrected to 0x6806D0. At the wrong value it pointed into 0xE806D0, which is not a function start, and buildFindings rejected it.

addresses.name: GetText
addresses.comment: **The localisation lookup.** Both arguments are pushed and the callee cleans them (`ret 8`). **It does not answer with a string** - the out is the sixteen byte text object, the entry plus a vector of the $VARIABLE$ replacements to apply, and characters come out of CInternationalizedText::Render. A key it cannot find gets an empty entry made for it rather than an error. Province names are localisation too, under `PROV<id>`; the game builds that key with the format string at `0x11BE118`. The name is BiceLib's.

addresses.name: CInternationalizedText::Render
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __thiscall CInternationalizedText::Render(CInternationalizedText* this@ECX, Hoi3CString* out@ESI, CTextRenderColours colours@stack:4) @EAX
addresses.comment: **A text object to characters.** `thiscall` on the object with sixteen bytes of colour settings pushed by value (`ret 0x10`), and the built string handed back in **esi** - the same register trick as the key in CInternationalizedText::Replace. It writes the length and capacity over whatever the out string held, so it must be given an empty one. The name is BiceLib's.

addresses.name: CInternationalizedText::Replace
addresses.signature: void __thiscall CInternationalizedText::Replace(CInternationalizedText* this@ECX, Hoi3CString* key@ESI, Hoi3CString* value@stack:4)
addresses.comment: **`text.Replace(key, value)`**, the `$NAME$` style variable mechanism: the text in ecx, the value pushed, and **the key in esi**, which the compiler left in a register variable and the callee reads from there (`mov edx, esi` at `0x682F7A`, and pushed outright at `0x682F90`). It builds a 0x40 byte object - vftable, the text at `+4`, the key as a string at `+8` and the value as another at `+0x24`, both copied - so a value need not outlive the call. `ret 4`. The name is BiceLib's.

addresses.name: AddTextEntry
addresses.signature: void __stdcall AddTextEntry(void* database, Hoi3CString* key, Hoi3CString* text)
addresses.comment: Puts an entry in the localisation database under a key. Also what the lookup calls when a key is **missing** - it creates an empty entry so the renderer can say NO_TEXT_FOR_KEY, which is why a missing key answers without failing. The name is BiceLib's.

addresses.name: ReleaseTextReplacements
addresses.comment: Destroys the replacements a text object collected, walking the vector whose three pointers are handed in **edi** and calling slot 0 of each entry's table with 1. The caller frees the block afterwards. A lookup that added no variables has none, so the loop runs no times. The name is BiceLib's.

addresses.name: Session::Session
addresses.comment: vftable 0x15FE5E8, 8 slots, no RTTI; 'session.cpp'. ret 0x84. Builds the command channel by mode - 0 -> 0x737100, 1 -> 0x734550, 2 -> 0x73BE00, other -> 0x73C4D0 - and stores it at [this+0x38]. A sibling overload is at rva 0x688200. Instance counter at 0x1BEA4F0.
addresses.signature: void * Session::Session(void *this, Hoi3CString name, Hoi3CString address, int mode, int, int, int, int, int)

addresses.name: Session::BindChannel
addresses.comment: Sets [session+0x38]=channel, [channel+0x1C]=session, [session+0x230]=100 (the executed-serial history cap), [session+0x2C]=4, and the gate byte: [session+0x34]=1 for mode 1 or 2, 0 otherwise. Channel and session come in in ecx and edx, the rest on the stack.

addresses.name: Session::PumpCommands
addresses.comment: session.cpp. THE OTHER HALF OF THE CHOKE POINT. Switches on [session+0x2C], pumps the channel (slot 7), takes its pending list (slot 8), and for each command checks slot 14 and calls CCommand::Execute (slot 6) at rva 0x689940. Logs 'Executing command ' <type id> <serial> when byte 0x1A857BE is set. Holds 'Atempted to execute invalid order with stamp ' and 'Command double! Skipping.'. 23 direct callers. ret 4.

addresses.name: CommandExecute_CallSite
addresses.comment: call eax, where eax = [command_vftable+0x18] = CCommand::Execute. The one Execute call site in the command-queue path, inside Session::PumpCommands. Hook here to see every command the game runs.

addresses.name: ApplicationInstallsObservable
addresses.comment:
`mov dword ptr [esi+0xE4], edi` inside the base CApplication constructor 0x6909A0, which CEU3Application::CEU3Application (0x22F080) calls at 0x22F0F3 - **the only write to CEU3Application +0xE4 in the image.** edi is a 0xC0-byte object allocated at 0x690AD2, constructed by 0x732CB0, and given five vftables: 0x15FDDC0 at +0 and 0x15FDE20/0x15FDE30/0x15FDE40/0x15FDE50 at +0x18/+0x30/+0x48/+0x60. None has RTTI, so the class is unidentified; only slot 4 was resolved, and it is the shared empty stub 0x20CD50.

That `esi` is the application is self-evident from the same function zeroing +0x88 at 0x690AAA and +0xE0 at 0x690ACC - the pair CEU3Application::SetNextScreen writes and CEU3Application::Run reads - which independently confirms that CInGameIdler +0x1790 is the CEU3Application.

**Trap 12 warning attached to this offset:** 0x2913F0 writes +0xE0, +0xE4, +0xF4 and +0xF8 in the same shape and is NOT the application - it constructs a CIngameLobby (vftable 0x15CFBA4, base CReferenceObject 0x15C3AE4, CSessionInfoObserver sub-object at +0x30). Four matching displacements in the same address band is not an identification. And +0xE4 is not +0x124, the still-unidentified field CInGameIdler slot 15 (0x24D7C0) returns. See reversing/FINDINGS-resetpath.md section 3(a).

addresses.name: CEU3Application::SetNextScreen
addresses.comment: Sets this->+0x88 = 1 and this->+0xE0 = the new screen, releasing whatever was pending. Receiver in ESI. Two callers: 0x6329F8, in LoadEverything at stage 17 immediately after CFrontEnd::CFrontEnd (0x6ED660) and the 'Idler Initialised <' line, and 0x6F1231. The run loop picks the pending screen up on its next pass.

addresses.name: CEU3Application::Run
addresses.signature: void __fastcall CEU3Application::Run(CEU3Application* this@EDI, int unknown1@stack:4, int unknown2@stack:8)
addresses.comment: The run loop main.cpp:601 calls. Takes the application in EDI and never writes edi - trap 11 again. Pins the process to one CPU through GetProcessAffinityMask/SetThreadAffinityMask, calls vftable slot 7 (which for CEU3Application is the shared empty stub 0xABF890, so nothing), then loops 0xA910A1..0xA9142D until this->+0xF8 == 0x12. Per frame it calls slot 1 of the current screen at 0xA9138D; the pending-screen swap at 0xA913A0 runs only when this->+0x88 is set, and that block calls the incoming screen's slot 2, then SLOT 3 at 0xA9140C, then slot 5. That is how CFrontEnd slot 3 (0x6EEF00) is reached, and it is why slot 3 is a one-shot activation hook rather than per-frame work. Signature corrected 2026-10-02 by the signature audit (reversing/findings/FINDINGS-sigaudit.md).

addresses.name: CEU3Application::LoadKey
addresses.signature: void __thiscall CEU3Application::LoadKey(CEU3Application* this, CParseContext* parse, SaveToken key)
addresses.comment: One key, `name` - the application settings file. Token 0x1A, read by ParseString into `this + 0x8C`.

addresses.name: ReturnTrue
addresses.comment: `mov al, 1; ret` - the compiler-folded true predicate, in **440 vftable slots across 259 classes**. Trap 4: not to be named after a class. See ReturnFalse (0x192360) for the land/naval/air predicate triple it forms with it.

addresses.name: LoadKey_CommandThunk
addresses.signature: void __stdcall LoadKey_CommandThunk(void* this@ECX, CParseContext* parse, SaveToken key)
addresses.comment: Four instructions into the already-named CCommand::LoadKey. Five sibling commands share this one body - CClearBookmark, CLobbyStartGame, CQuit, CReopenLobby and CStartGame - so CQuit, which it was recorded as, was an arbitrary pick among them. A four-instruction frame-only thunk that tail jumps into `CCommand::LoadKey` (`0x67BC80`), which is what compares the key's **text** rather than its token - that is why the switch reader finds nothing. The body is shared by five sibling command classes: CClearBookmark, CLobbyStartGame, CQuit, CReopenLobby and CStartGame.

addresses.name: FixedPointSqrt
addresses.comment: A square root in thousandths: zero for a non-positive input, an initial guess of value/2 for large values, then Newton iterations on `g - (g*g/1000 - value)/(2g)`. Read as structure and **not evaluated**, so the name is inference. Used by GetCategoryResearchAbility (rva 0x1332B0) to damp a practical above 6.000.

addresses.name: CReferenceObject::LoadKey
addresses.signature: void __thiscall CReferenceObject::LoadKey(CReferenceObject* this, CParseContext* parse, SaveToken key)
addresses.comment: **One key, `id` (token 11)**, read as an object id pair into `this + 8`; everything else goes straight to ReportUnknownKey. Nineteen classes inherit it, CMinister and CRebelFaction among them, which is where their `id_type` at 0x8 and `id` at 0xC come from.

addresses.name: FindPersistentById
addresses.comment:
Looks a saved object up by its type and id - the two halves of the `id = { type = N id = N }` pair the save writes. Type 0x25 is a leader: CKillLeaderEffect::GetLeader calls it with that and the id from the event file. The name is BiceLib's.

**It takes both arguments in registers and nothing on the stack.** EAX holds the address of the key pair - two dwords, `{type, id}` - and ECX holds the hash table; the result comes back in EAX and is NULL when nothing matches. All 427 call sites set EAX with a `lea` of a stack local in the instruction immediately before the call and push nothing at all, and none of them cleans any stack afterwards.

The body: `edi = [eax]` (type), `esi = [eax+4]` (id), hashes `(type << 16) + id` by dividing it by `[ecx+4]` (the bucket count) and indexes `[ecx+8]` (the bucket array) with the remainder, then walks the chain - `[node]` is the stored pointer, `[node+4]` the next node - comparing `[stored+8]` against the type and `[stored+0xC]` against the id. So the registered object keeps its own copy of the key pair at +8/+0xC, which is where CReferenceObject's unread +0x8 and +0xC most likely go - that last step is inference, not something checked.

The table is one of two globals, `[0x1A857F4]` and `[0x1A857F0]`, and 374 of the 427 sites choose between them with `cmp <type>, 0x1268` immediately before - so the type space is split into two registries at 4712. 132 of the 427 sites follow the call with `add eax, -8` before using the result; what that adjustment reaches has not been settled here.

addresses.name: CIcon::CIcon
addresses.comment: Writes CIcon's vftable 0x15FFC68 at [this] and 0x15FFD94 at [this+0x48]. Identified from CEU3Minimap::CEU3Minimap (rva 0x27A3C0), which calls it at 0x67A47D and then writes 0x15CF15C at offset 0; CEU3Minimap's RTTI base chain is CIcon < CButton < TButton < CGuiObject. For an icon the CGuiObject subobject is at offset 0, unlike a window. `ret 0x38`, but the argument boundaries were not read, so no signature is claimed.

addresses.name: MT19937NextFloat01
addresses.comment: 0xAA2B20, bare ret, the generator in ecx, a float in [0,1) returned in st0. Calls MT19937Next, masks with 0x7FFFFFFF (redundantly - see MT19937Next) and multiplies by the double 2^-31 at 0x160A2B8. This is the form the daily event pass uses through its own inlined copy.

addresses.name: MT19937NextThousandths
addresses.comment: 0xAA2B50, ret 4, the generator in ecx and an int* out on the stack. Draws, takes the remainder mod 1000 and returns remainder * 1000 / 1000000 - a fraction in thousandths with only three distinct significant digits of entropy. 0xAA2FD0 is the same thing on the global generator.

addresses.name: MT19937Next
addresses.comment:
0xAA2B90, bare ret, the MT19937 state in eax, the tempered draw out in eax. Twists through 0xAA2C80 when the index at state+0x9C0 (= 0x1711940) is zero, then tempers: y ^= y>>11; y ^= (y<<7) & 0x9D2C5680; y ^= (y<<15) & 0xEFC60000; y ^= y>>18 - the two masks appear pre-shifted as 0xFF3A58AD and 0xFFFFDF8C, and the index advances mod 0x270 (624). **Both right shifts are arithmetic (sar at 0xAA2BAD and 0xAA2BD7), not logical, so bit 31 of the result is always zero and the draw is always in [0, 0x7FFFFFFF].** That is why the engine's ubiquitous signed `Random() % N` cannot produce a negative remainder, and why 0xAA2B20's `and eax, 0x7FFFFFFF` is redundant. Do not 'fix' a `% N` site on the theory that the draw can be negative.

**The apply script cannot create this function in a project where Ghidra has already swallowed it.** 0xAA2B10 is a two-instruction thunk - `mov eax, ecx; jmp 0xAA2B90` with int3 padding at 0xAA2B17 - and Ghidra follows that tail jump and absorbs the target into the thunk's body, so an apply reports `inside CSimpleRandom::GetInteger (entry 00AA2B10) - boundaries need a look`. The finding is the correct one: 0xAA2B90 is also reached by a direct `call` at 0xAA2B26, so it is a function in its own right. To take the name, split the body - delete the function at 0xAA2B10, let the script make both, or run `ResetBiceLibFunction.java 0x00aa2b10` first. Everything else in the same build applies cleanly; this is the only entry in 1885 that does not.

addresses.name: MT19937Twist
addresses.comment: 0xAA2C80, the MT19937 state in edi, no arguments and nothing returned: the 624-word twist, run by MT19937Next and by every function that inlines a draw whenever g_random_index is zero. **This is not a faithful MT19937 and two deviations are visible in the bytes.** (1) The twist constant is **0x9908B0DF**, not the standard 0x9908B00D - `xor edx, 0x9908b0df` at 0xAA2CE5, 0xAA2D34, 0xAA2D81 and 0xAA2DCF, the four copies of the unrolled loop. (2) The `y >> 1` uses `sar` (0xAA2CCA, 0xAA2D19, 0xAA2D67, 0xAA2DB4), not a logical shift, so a negative y propagates its sign. The rest is standard: y is assembled as `((state[k] ^ x) & 0x7FFFFFFF) ^ x`, the index walks mod 0x270 (624) and the offset is 0x18C/0x18D (397). Anyone reimplementing the game's RNG - to predict a roll or to reproduce a save - must use 0x9908B0DF and arithmetic shifts, or the sequence will not match.

addresses.name: ReseedGlobalRandom
addresses.comment: 0xAA2ED0. Re-initialises the global generator from the seed at 0x174DA94 through 0xAA2BF0 with g_random_seed (0x1710F80) in ecx, and zeroes the index at 0x1711940. Two callers: RunHourlyTick at 0x681C79 and 0x6D7BF2. 0xAA2BF0 itself was not read, so 'reseed' is read off the shape - the seed global, the index reset - rather than from the initialiser.

addresses.name: Random
addresses.comment: 0xAA2F80, no arguments, returns a non-negative int in eax. addresses.name: CEU3BitmapFont::Load
addresses.comment:
**Loads the font**, virtual slot 5. Builds `gfx/fonts/` + `fontName` + `.tga`, loads that texture, then calls CEU3BitmapFont::LoadGlyphs for the `.fnt` beside it.

**It and LoadGlyphs have no padding between them**, so reversing/image.py's functionStart answers 0x6F9EA0 for addresses in either. The frames tell them apart: this one reserves 0x58 bytes and the parser 0x1B4, and the parser addresses [ebp - 0x1C0], which this frame could not hold.

addresses.name: CEU3BitmapFont::LoadGlyphs
addresses.comment:
**Reads `gfx/fonts/<fontName>.fnt` into the font's glyph table.** The file is an AngelCode BMFont descriptor in plain text, and this **never reads its key names**: it matches only the first token of a line - `char` at 0x6FA2E3, `kerning` at 0x6FA4AC - and then takes the numbers after it in file order, one atoi each.

`char` gives id, x, y, width, height, xoffset, yoffset, xadvance, in that order, into a fresh 0x820 byte CEU3BitmapFontGlyph stored at `font + id * 4 + 0x94`. An id of 0x20 has its height forced to zero at 0x6FA3BD whatever the file says. `kerning` gives first, second, amount, and appends {second, amount} to the glyph named first.

That the parse is positional is why `xadvance` appears nowhere in the executable, and why the numbers in the .fnt are the ones the renderer advances by.

No `this`: the font arrives as the single stack argument and the ECX the caller had is unused, so it is __stdcall despite living on the class.

addresses.name: CEU3BitmapFont::GetStringWidth
addresses.signature: int __thiscall CEU3BitmapFont::GetStringWidth(CEU3BitmapFont* this, const char* text, int length)
addresses.comment:
**How wide a string draws, in pixels**, virtual slot 10. A negative `length` means to the NUL.

Each byte adds its glyph's xadvance and then the kerning pair between it and **the literal next byte** - the game does not skip an escape to find the next drawn character. A glyph the font does not list adds nothing.

The escapes: 0xA7 and the byte after it are skipped, but only where the virtual at +0x4C says this font handles them; 0x40 takes three bytes and adds an icon width from the virtual at +0x68; 0xA3 takes a [A-Za-z_] name and adds one from +0x64; 0xA4 adds a flat 8; `{` adds 8 and takes two bytes.

A newline ends a line rather than the string, and the return is the widest line.

BiceLib's Text::Font follows all of this except the icon escapes, which it measures as ordinary glyphs because nothing it writes contains one.

addresses.name: DestroyStringsInRange
addresses.comment:
**Empties the string at the start of every record in a range**, walking `[first, last)` in steps of **0x20** and giving each string's buffer back where it had one - `if (capacity >= 0x10) free(data)`, then capacity 0xF, length 0, first byte 0. Both ends arrive in registers, first in eax and last in edi. `ret`.

It is a destructor loop the compiler wrote once and **1552 call sites share**: every record type of 0x20 bytes that begins with a string folds onto this one body, which is why its callers have nothing to do with each other. The stride is baked in, so it is only correct for that shape.

BiceLib meets it tearing a text object down: after ReleaseTextReplacements has destroyed the object each replacement points at, this empties the name each one carries, and the caller frees the block. The name is BiceLib's.

Held at slot 18 by two `.rdata` tables - 0x15E3F44, which the RTTI export names `CWeatherBillboardType`, and **0x1605258**, which it does not name and which is therefore `CBillboardType`'s own. addresses.name: LogSink::Write
addresses.signature: void __thiscall LogSink::Write(LogSink* this, int channel, Hoi3CString* file, int line, Hoi3CString* message)
addresses.comment: **Where every message in the game arrives.** The record's destructor pulls the four apart and calls this through the sink's vftable slot 1. It opens with a filter of its own - `call 0x40C3C0` on a global at `0x16052F0`, taking the message and dropping it when that answers true - and only then picks a file by channel. **Measured, 2026-09-20**, by catching a whole startup: `3` writes to `system.log`, `0x10000` to `setup.log`, `0x10002` to `game.log`, `0x10006` to `time.log`, and every channel the run produced reached a file. `0x10004`, which carries the three `Unknown History Command` sites, was never produced at all. **Hooked once, on 2026-09-20**, with a five byte jump over the prologue (`55 8B EC 6A FF`) - ahead of the filter, so every message built was seen. That capture matched `setup.log` and `game.log` line for line, which is how the filter was shown to drop nothing, and the hook was then removed as redundant. `ret 0x10`.
